papers.title: PZLS-1/PDZRN controls muscle polarity downstream of Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling in C. elegans muscles
papers.abstract: Non-canonical Wnt pathways provide directional cues for cell polarity, but the mechanisms that translate these cues into asymmetric cellular organisation remain incompletely defined. We previously showed that a non-canonical EGL-20/Wnt-CAM-1/Ror-DSH-1/Dishevelled pathway establishes polarised membrane compartments in Caenorhabditis elegans body wall muscles. However, how EGL-20/Wnt signalling is translated into muscle polarity remains unknown. Here, we identify PZLS-1, the C. elegans ortholog of human PDZRN3, PDZRN4 and PDZD4, as a regulator of muscle polarity. Although PDZRN proteins are known targets of non-canonical Wnt-Ror signalling, how they are spatially organised within polarised cells and how their protein domains contribute to their function remain largely unknown. We reveal that PZLS-1 is itself asymmetrically localised by Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling, and is closely associated with DSH-1. PZLS-1 and DSH-1 colocalise in intracellular puncta and are mutually required for their localisation. In vivo structure-function analyses reveal conserved protein motifs that differentially control PZLS-1 localisation, abundance and function. This includes a previously uncharacterized highly conserved sequence that regulates PZLS-1 abundance in a DSH-1-dependent manner. We further show that PZLS 1 and DSH-1 control the abundance and polarised localisation of VAB-8/KIF26b, another conserved target of Wnt-Ror signalling. Together, these findings indicate that Wnt-Ror-Dvl signalling can control the spatial organisation and abundance of PDZRN- and KIF26B-family proteins in vivo, providing a mechanism to translate extracellular polarity cues into intracellular asymmetry.

papers.title: SorCS2 controls Wnt signaling homeostasis during neurodevelopment by regulating Ror2 activity and trafficking
papers.abstract: Wnt signaling orchestrates key developmental processes, yet mechanisms restricting its spatial and temporal activity remain incompletely understood. Here we identify SorCS2, a VPS10p-domain sorting receptor, as a conserved regulator of Wnt signaling homeostasis. Integrating proteomics, cell biology, embryology, and vertebrate models, we show that SorCS2 interacts with the noncanonical Wnt receptor Ror2 and controls its trafficking, Wnt5a-induced internalization, and lysosomal degradation. In mouse dopaminergic progenitors, SorCS2 deficiency enhances responsiveness to canonical and noncanonical Wnt ligands, increases Ror2 phosphorylation, and amplifies downstream signaling of both Wnt signaling cascades. Loss of SorCS2 further disrupts the ligand-receptor feedback loop, leading to elevated Ror2, Wnt5a, and Wnt1 expression, accelerated proliferation and neurogenesis, and increased expression of Tcf4, a gene implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. Across vertebrate systems, SorCS2-dependent control of Ror2 signaling is required for anterior-posterior axis elongation, convergent extension, somitogenesis, and brain morphogenesis. These findings define a SorCS2-dependent sorting mechanism that fine-tunes morphogen receptor signaling during vertebrate neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Single-Cell Multimodal Profiling Reveals Maternal Diabetes-Nkx2-5 Interaction in Congenital Heart Disease in a Genetic Model Recapitulating Human Embryopathies
papers.abstract: The etiological complexity of congenital heart disease (CHD) arises from the interaction between genetic and environmental factors. We hypothesized that environmental exposure could potentiate a genetic susceptibility, leading to an increased incidence of specific cardiac defects. To test this hypothesis, we used betaV59M+ female mice exhibiting severe hyperglycemia (>28 mmol/L) without dyslipidemia, a model we characterized that faithfully recapitulates human diabetic embryopathy. These females were crossed with males haploinsufficient for Nkx2-5, a transcription factor essential for cardiac development and implicated in human CHD. Our results show that the combination of genetic susceptibility and a hyperglycemic maternal environment (GxE) leads to a higher frequency and severity of cardiac malformations, including ventricular septal defects specifically involving the muscular septum, univentricular morphologies, and dilation with thinning of the myocardium. These structural abnormalities were associated with transcriptional changes affecting the contractile identity of the chamber myocardium. Single-nucleus multiomic profiling (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq) of the E9.5 cardiac region revealed that the interaction between maternal diabetes and Nkx2-5 haploinsufficiency profoundly reshapes transcriptional and chromatin accessibility landscapes. These changes affect not only metabolic pathways, but also cell cycle progression in second heart field (SHF) progenitors, likely contributing to the observed structural cardiac defects. Multiomic integration further identifies a disrupted indirect Nkx2-5-Aldh1a2 regulatory axis in posterior SHF progenitors, while demonstrating that maternal diabetes selectively affects a restricted subset of Nkx2-5-dependent regulatory elements associated with cardiomyocyte maturation. Our findings establish a comprehensive single-cell multiomic resource that will facilitate the integration of human GWAS and other genomic datasets, enabling the identification and functional interpretation of disease-associated loci.

papers.title: Plakoglobin supports length-dependent force generation and cardiac resistance to fasting
papers.abstract: Mechanical activity protects muscle from atrophy, but how contractile forces relate to anabolic signaling remains unclear. We previously showed that plakoglobin promotes insulin-PI3K-AKT-FoxO signaling and that its loss causes skeletal muscle atrophy. Here, super-resolution microscopy revealed that plakoglobin localizes with desmin at the sarcolemma and is lost from the membrane during fasting-induced skeletal muscle atrophy. In skinned muscle fibers, plakoglobin downregulation impaired stretch-induced increase in myofilament activation at long sarcomere length. During fasting, skeletal muscle lost sarcolemmal plakoglobin-containing complexes, insulin signaling, and mass and induced MuRF1 and MAFbx/Atrogin1. In contrast, cardiac muscle retained these complexes and anabolic signaling, and maintained its mass. Cardiac plakoglobin also resisted AAV-shJUP-mediated depletion despite viral delivery. Moreover, MEK inhibition disrupted this cardiac response, reduced AKT signaling, induced atrogenes, and decreased cardiac mass. Thus, plakoglobin supports force generation at increased sarcomere length, and preservation of plakoglobin-containing complexes and MEK-ERK signaling accompany cardiac resistance to fasting-induced atrophy.

papers.title: Continuous Large Maf Activity Maintains Fast Myofiber Identity and Multicellular Homeostasis in Adult Skeletal Muscle
papers.abstract: Fast myofibers are preferentially affected during aging, exhibiting atrophy and shifts toward slower myofiber programs, yet the mechanisms preserving established fast-fiber identity remain unclear. Here, we show that the large Maf transcription factors Mafa, Mafb, and Maf are continuously required to maintain type IIb myofiber identity in adult skeletal muscle. Inducible deletion of large Mafs caused near-complete loss of type IIb fibers, a transition toward type IIx/IIa states, reduced strength, and increased fatigue resistance. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq revealed transcriptional and chromatin accessibility remodeling across the fast myosin locus, characterized by persistent loss of Myh4 expression and increased accessibility around Myh1. Single-nucleus RNA-seq identified transient myonuclei co-expressing multiple myosin isoforms before emergence of a Myh1-dominant state, accompanied by remodeling of non-myonuclear cell populations. These changes shared features with aging- and denervation-associated muscle remodeling. Thus, continuous large Maf activity maintains adult fast myofiber identity and coordinates skeletal muscle tissue homeostasis.

papers.title: Histone H2A.X contributes to Gene Expression Regulation and Cell-Cycle Progression in Toxoplasma gondii Tachyzoites
papers.abstract: Histone H2A.X is a conserved variant classically associated with the DNA damage response (DDR), where its phosphorylation ({gamma}H2A.X) marks double-strand breaks and recruits repair factors. H2A.X is absent in many parasitic protozoans such as Plasmodium, Trypanosoma and Leishmania. In Toxoplasma gondii, the obligate intracellular parasite, causative agent of toxoplasmosis, however, its presence raises the question of whether it contributes to genome stability. To tackle this, we generated a T. gondii knockout of H2A.X (RH{Delta}H2A.X) and evaluated its phenotype. Although H2A.X is phosphorylated in response to DNA damage in T. gondii as in other systems, RH{Delta}H2A.X parasites showed no increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, indicating that H2A.X is dispensable for canonical DDR. Instead, loss of H2A.X caused reduced gliding motility, increased host cell invasion and clustering of extracellular parasites after egress. Despite no defects in replication rate, RH{Delta}H2A.X showed delayed mitotic progression with abnormal vacuole morphology. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a moderate yet coordinated reprogramming of protein-coding genes. Specifically, H2A.X loss altered the expression of key apical secretory and virulence factors, especially ROP18, while inducing the transcriptional activation of mitotic and DNA replication machinery. Differential enrichment analysis further revealed that upregulated genes were preferentially associated with S phase, whereas downregulated genes were enriched during mitosis and cytokinesis. This is consistent with the delayed mitotic progression and spindle abnormalities observed by microscopy and flow cytometry and suggests a cell cycle phase-specific mechanism of H2A.X-dependent transcriptional control. Rather than a driver of DDR, these findings suggest that T. gondii H2A.X operates as a chromatin organizer that coordinates cell division fidelity and virulence gene expression.

papers.title: A role for CIZ1, a Nuclear Matrix Protein Overexpressed in Cancer Cells, in Controlling the Initiation of DNA Replication
papers.abstract: DNA replication licensing is tightly coordinated with cell-cycle progression to ensure genome stability. Here we demonstrate that CIZ1, a nuclear matrix scaffold protein in human cells, coordinates DNA replication licensing through direct interactions with the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC), CDC6, and Cyclins E/A-CDK2. The C-terminal zinc finger region of CIZ1 mediates binding to the cyclin-binding motifs of ORC1 and CDC6, and Cyclin -CDK-dependent phosphorylation regulates these interactions. Cell cycle analyses demonstrated a dynamic association of CIZ1 with ORC1 and CDC6. Functional studies showed that CIZ1 depletion impaired MCM loading, reduced DNA synthesis, delayed S-phase progression and inhibited cell proliferation. Cancer cells overexpressing CIZ1 exhibited an enhanced dependency on its expression, and CRISPR tiling screens identified the C-terminal regulatory region containing cyclin-binding motifs and CDK phosphorylation sites as essential for cell proliferation. Acute degradation of CIZ1 further revealed an unexpected role in maintaining CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) occupancy at specific genomic loci and regulating transcriptional programs associated with cell adhesion and migration, indicating that CIZ1 links DNA replication with higher-order genome organization. Finally, depletion of CIZ1 significantly suppressed colorectal tumor growth in xenograft models. Together, these findings establish CIZ1 as a multifunctional scaffold that integrates DNA replication licensing, Cyclin -CDK signaling, and chromatin architecture.

papers.title: Common cis-eQTLs do not explain chromosome 21 expression deviations from the ploidy expectation in Down syndrome
papers.abstract: Down syndrome (DS) results from trisomy 21 (T21), the triplication of human chromosome 21 (HSA21). On average, genes on HSA21 are overexpressed at the expected 1.5-fold increase. A small subset of HSA21 genes is expressed closer to euploid levels. Could local genetic regulatory variation explain deviations from the expected dosage? Using the largest DS-specific transcriptomic dataset to date from the Human Trisome Project (HTP) and GTEx expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs), we tested whether local genetic regulatory variation contributes to gene-specific buffering or amplification of HSA21 dosage effects in DS. We compared the bulk RNA-seq profiles of protein-coding genes, lncRNAs, and pseudogenes from whole-blood samples of 274 participants with T21 and 80 euploid (D21) participants. We filtered out genes with low read counts or high genomic repeat content and applied ploidy correction to the differential expression analysis. We found 13 genes that differed significantly from the expected fold change. We cross-referenced GTEx whole-blood eQTLs (cis window 1 {+/-} Mb) with the 13 deviating genes. A common cis-eQTL was detected for 8 of the 10 testable genes. However, 59 of 99 HSA21 genes that had the expected fold change had significant cis-eQTLs. Additionally, T21 participants carry the eQTL alleles at similar frequencies to GTEx donors. Therefore, cis-eQTLs explain differences between people with T21, not the difference between T21 and D21. Overall, common cis-regulatory variation acts on HSA21 genes in T21 as it does in euploid blood, but it does not explain which genes deviate from the ploidy expectation.

papers.title: Multistage AI Crop Inspection and Segmentation Framework (MACISF)
papers.abstract: Crop quality assessment is one of the most critical components of modern agriculture, which directly influences yield optimization, post-harvest management, and food security. Conventional evaluation of field crops relies on manual inspection, which is time-consuming, subjective, and unscalable. This paper proposes the Multistage AI Crop Inspection and Segmentation Framework (MACISF), an automated multistage deep learning pipeline for fruit quality evaluation from visual features. The pipeline is comprised of three stages: (i) an EfficientNetV2-L backbone, fine-tuned with a three-stage progressive strategy, for crop type classification; (ii) seven species-specific EfficientNetV2-S classifiers for healthy-versusdefective detection; and (iii) a YOLOv8m module for defect localization. Trained and evaluated on a composite dataset spanning seven fruit species, MACISF achieves 99.23% crop type accuracy (macro F1-score 99.23%, macro AUC-ROC 0.993), 99.39% mean health state accuracy with 99.51% mean defective-class recall, and a projected grading mAP@0.5 of 92.3%. On crop type classification, the Stage 1 classifier is second only to InceptionV3 (by 0.15 percentage points) among seven models trained on the same data, and outperforms ResNet-50, Xception, EfficientNetB3, DenseNet-121, and MobileNetV2. Unlike these singletask baseline models, MACISF additionally delivers health-state assessment, defect severity grading, and a per-unit economic and nutritional evaluation. Results are reported on heldout test data from a controlled dataset, and field validation is left for future work.

papers.title: Spatial context of cellular heterogeneity in triple-negative breast cancer reveals actionable subtypes
papers.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive, heterogeneous disease with limited targeted treatment options. Leveraging bulk and spatial transcriptomics and cellular mapping of breast tissue from a large patient cohort, we identified three reproducible TNBC ecosystem subtypes that encode distinct spatial tumor-microenvironment architectures and clinically relevant treatment-response phenotype. Our analyses define: (1) an immune-exhausted subtype associated with immune checkpoint therapy (ICT); (2) a highly fibrotic/hypoxic subtype; and (3) a metabolically reprogrammed subtype characterized by nuclear-receptor and fatty-acid signaling. Spatial profiling further revealed subtype-specific organization of epithelial, immune, and stromal programs across tumor centers and invasive edges. Multiplexed imaging independently supported the contrasting immune-infiltrated and stromal-excluded architectures of the immune-engaged and fibrotic subtypes. The unique markers associated with the subtypes also provide the basis for subtyping and candidate therapeutic vulnerabilities. Our study provides a robust framework for personalized medicine, highlighting that targeting specific spatio-cellular architectures is critical to improving clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Apical-Out Ileal Organoids: A Versatile Platform for Probing Gut-Nanomaterial Interactions
papers.abstract: The human ileal epithelium forms a critical interface governing interactions with luminal microorganisms and nanomaterials, yet physiologically relevant in vitro models with accessible apical surfaces remain limited. Here, human apical-out ileoids derived from healthy ileal biopsies are established as a platform that recapitulates the architecture and complexity of the native ileal epithelium. Assessment of donor- and passage-dependent variability identifies a representative ileoid line and a robust culture window. Integrated proteomic, imaging, ultrastructural, and functional analyses demonstrate preservation of key epithelial features, including brush-border organization, barrier integrity, absorptive capacity, and multiple endocytic pathways. Intact ileoids internalize nanoparticles of distinct surface charge, including empty lipid nanoparticles compositionally matched to approved mRNA vaccine formulations, establishing that uptake can be quantified across an unperturbed apical surface. This uptake is restrained by a retained mucin-rich glycocalyx. Cleavage of surface-attached mucins selectively enhances uptake of negatively charged nanoparticles, leaving near-neutral and positively charged nanoparticles unchanged, and increasing entry of Salmonella bacteria. These findings reveal the glycocalyx as a charge-selective regulator of epithelial uptake. In conclusion, our study provides a foundation for nanoparticle-epithelium investigations using human apical-out ileoids, and a versatile, translationally relevant platform for nanomedicine delivery, host-microbe interactions, and epithelial transport.

papers.title: Escape from replicative crisis and immortalization precedes complex genome evolution
papers.abstract: Shortening of telomeres restricts the proliferative capacity of human somatic cells by inducing replicative senescence and crisis. During cancerous transformation, premalignant cells must overcome these barriers and acquire replicative immortality. Single-cell DNA strand-specific genome sequencing of crisis cells revealed extreme genome instability characterized by complex chromosomal abnormalities. Unexpectedly, spontaneously emerging postcrisis clones showed relatively few and simple structural variants. However, with accumulating divisions following crisis escape, the genomes of immortal postcrisis clones evolve and amass genomic alterations, including tetraploidization events with subsequent losses and gains of individual chromosomes. Our data point towards a new model of tumorigenesis in which crisis acts as a strong selective barrier against cells with aberrant karyotypes, and in which high karyotypic complexity is acquired after immortalization and crisis escape.

papers.title: Ultrastructural Analysis of Extracellular Vesicles and Surface Protrusions from the Parasite Tritrichomonas foetus
authors: R. C. B. Q. de Figueiredo
papers.abstract: Tritrichomonas foetus is an extracellular flagellated protist responsible for bovine and feline tritrichomonosis, yet several aspects of its cell biology and pathogenicity remain poorly understood. Here, we evaluated the presence of extracellular vesicles (EVs) and membrane protrusions in T. foetus using complementary electron microscopy and immunolabeling approaches. EV-like structures of different sizes were found protruding from the parasite cell body and anterior flagella, and ultrathin sections showed continuity between the membranes of these protrusions and the plasma or flagellar membrane. Multivesicular bodies containing intraluminal vesicles were also observed, and an EV-enriched fraction isolated from conditioned medium contained vesicles with a broad size distribution, consistent with heterogeneous EV populations. Immunofluorescence further showed tetraspanin-1 in intracellular vesicles, flagella, and vesicular structures protruding from the parasite surface. Exposure to bovine preputial epithelial cells resulted in a ninefold increase in the percentage of parasites displaying flagellar cytoneme-like structures, suggesting a possible role for these projections in host-parasite interactions. VPS32, a component of the ESCRT-III machinery, was found in intraluminal vesicles, vesicles protruding from the cell body and flagella, isolated EVs, and flagellar membrane protrusions. In parasites overexpressing VPS32, the number of vesicles per flagellum increased, and the percentage of cells with flagellar cytoneme-like projections was fivefold higher than in control parasites. Pearling-like protrusions containing VPS32 were also observed. Together, these findings provide ultrastructural evidence for heterogeneous EV populations associated with the cell body and flagella of T. foetus and suggest that VPS32 could contribute to flagellar EV and membrane protrusion formation.

papers.title: A cell death-independent role for MLKL in TGF-β receptor recycling in Marfan syndrome
papers.abstract: Marfan syndrome (MFS) causes thoracic aortic aneurysm through mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene and subsequent dysregulated TGF-{beta} signalling. Mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein (MLKL) executes necroptosis after RIPK3-dependent phosphorylation, but also functions in endosomal trafficking. Here we show that MLKL phosphorylation sustains TGF-{beta} receptor recycling and aortic wall integrity without causing cell death. Phosphorylation-dead MLKLS345A/S347A (MlklAA) mice developed aortic root dilation with disorganised collagen architecture and a secretory-pathway proteomic signature. Crossing them with Fbn1C1039G/+ MFS mice aggravated aortic dilation, disrupted collagen fibril ultrastructure and prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation, and caused lethal rupture under angiotensin II. Complete MLKL deficiency reproduced this phenotype. Phosphorylated MLKL was increased in MFS aortas, yet cleaved caspase-3, TUNEL positivity, smooth muscle cell content and leukocyte infiltration were unchanged. In smooth muscle cells, MLKL depletion dysregulated collagen-modifying enzymes, altered TGF-{beta}-driven matrix remodelling and impaired RAB11-dependent TGF{beta}R1 recycling. These findings suggest that phosphorylation-dependent, non-lytic functions of MLKL may contribute to the maintenance of thoracic aortic integrity in MFS.

papers.title: The Arabidopsis outward K+ channel GORK mediates flg22-induced K+ efflux and stomatal closure
papers.abstract: Transient K+ efflux occurs rapidly following pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) perception by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) as part of pattern-triggered immunity (PTI). However, the molecular identities of the K+ channels responsible for PTI-associated K+ efflux and the mechanisms linking immune signaling to K+ channel regulation remain largely unknown. Here, we show that the channel GUARD CELL OUTWARD RECTIFYING K+ (GORK) is required for K+ efflux and stomatal closure induced by flg22, a model PAMP derived from bacterial flagellin. BOTRYTIS-INDUCED KINASE 1 (BIK1), a receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase associated with immune receptor complexes that functions as a central regulator of PTI, interacts with GORK and phosphorylates the channel on the conserved T199 residue in vitro. Electrophysiological analyses indicate that BIK1 inhibits GORK activity in a kinase-dependent manner and that T199 plays an essential role for GORK function. Together, this study identifies GORK as the key K+ channel executing rapid PTI-associated K+ efflux and associated stomatal closure, thus shedding light on the mechanisms of early immune signaling.

papers.title: Multi-omics reveals accumulation mechanisms underlying differences in sesquiterpenoid content across different growth environments of Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome
papers.abstract: This study aimed to explore mechanisms driving differential sesquiterpenoid accumulation in Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome (AMR) under different growth environments. Root and rhizosphere soil samples were collected from wild, imitated wild, one- and two-year cultivated AMR. Combined metabolomic, transcriptomic and microbiomic profiling was carried out to investigate alterations in sesquiterpenoid levels, root-associated microbiota, and terpenoid biosynthetic genes under different growth environments. Metabolomics revealed that wild AMR exhibited higher pyruvate consumption and accumulated more atractylone and atractylenolides. Transcriptomic analysis demonstrated that the genes encoding key MEP pathway enzymes (DXS, DXR, MCT, HDS) and the genes encoding the sesquiterpenoid biosynthetic enzyme GDS were significantly upregulated in wild AMR. In contrast, the genes encoding triterpenoid synthetic enzymes (SQS, SQE, {beta}-AS) were downregulated, redirecting metabolic precursors toward sesquiterpenoid synthesis. Microbial community structures differed substantially across groups. Further analysis suggested rhizosphere microorganisms were important contributors to AMR medicinal quality, and sesquiterpenoid metabolites accumulated in AMR roots, together with the rhizosphere microenvironment, jointly shape specific rhizosphere fungal assembly. This study systematically revealed the synergistic regulatory relationships among sesquiterpenoids metabolism, gene expression, growth environment, and root-associated microbes, providing multi-omics evidence for clarifying the mechanism by which these factors coordinately regulate the quality of AMR.

papers.title: Pan-cancer remodeling of reactive oxygen species homeostasis: distinct roles of the ROS-generation and antioxidant arms in immune context and outcome
papers.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are double-edged in cancer: tumor cells sustain high ROS generation while up-regulating antioxidant defense, so that the net balance between the two arms, rather than absolute ROS abundance, is the biologically meaningful quantity. Whether that balance defines a conserved tumor state across cancer types has been unclear. Here an experimentally measured ROS phenotype, obtained from a three-channel gold-nanocluster array, was generalized to public transcriptomes through a 107-gene ROS program scored in a large cell-line panel and in pan-cancer tumor and adjacent-normal tissue. The optical readout was reproducible and fully discriminative between cell lines, establishing the fingerprint as a quantitative starting point. In tumors, the generation and antioxidant arms were coordinately up-regulated relative to normal tissue, yet the two arms dissociated in their biology. The composite balance score tracked reduced immune infiltration consistently across cohorts, but arm-level decomposition showed that it was carried by low generation-arm activity in immune-cold tumors and followed arithmetically from how the balance score is defined; the association does not implicate antioxidant defense in immune infiltration. The clinical association pointed the other way: adverse outcome was attributable to the antioxidant arm, whereas generation was null. In cohort-held-out validation, tumors were separated from adjacent normal tissue, with redox programs outperforming generic phenotypic programs, indicating that the same program transfers across tumor types. Tumor remodeling of ROS homeostasis is therefore widespread, but its two arms carry distinct meanings: the balance score, driven by its generation term, reports immune context, whereas the antioxidant arm reports clinical risk.

papers.title: Spatially resolved tumor-microenvironment architecture defines therapeutic response in unresectable hepatoblastoma
papers.abstract: Background: Hepatoblastoma exhibits variable therapeutic response that is not fully explained by current risk stratification. While prior studies have characterized tumor composition, the role of spatial organization in determining outcome, particularly in unresectable disease requiring transplantation under immunosuppression, remains unclear. Methods: We integrated spatial transcriptomics using the 10x Genomics Visium platform (n = 11 tumors) with single-cell spatial molecular imaging using NanoString CosMx (n = 3 tumors) on post-chemotherapy explant specimens across clinically defined groups (relapse-prone unresectable, non-relapse unresectable, and resectable hepatoblastoma). Spatial deconvolution, module scoring, spatial co-localization, and cell-cell interaction analyses were used to define region-level transcriptional programs and their underlying cellular organization. Results: We identified three spatial architectures associated with clinical outcome. Relapse-prone tumors exhibited a centralized, TME-dominated organization enriched for progenitor-like, cycling, and stress-responsive tumor cell states co-localized with SPP1+ TAMs and CAFs, with enrichment of hypoxia response, extracellular matrix remodeling, and Midkine (MDK-LRP1) signaling. Non-relapse tumors displayed a distributed architecture with compartmentalized tumor-immune interactions, increased immune engagement, and preserved epithelial differentiation, including inflammatory hepatocyte-like states. Resection samples showed reduced tumor cell state heterogeneity and more uniform TME-immune organization. Conclusions: Integration of regional and single-cell spatial transcriptomics across two platforms reveals that the chemo-remodeled tumor architecture of hepatoblastoma encodes spatially organized tumor cell-TME interactions as central determinants of therapeutic response.

papers.title: TBX3 is required for the differentiation of a subset of retinal ganglion and cone photoreceptor cells
papers.abstract: Retinogenesis is a key step driving the formation of the neurons that later coordinate angiogenesis in the retina. Understanding these complex interactions requires dissecting apart its cellular and molecular drivers. To tease apart the molecular links coupling retinogenesis to vascular development, we utilized conditional knockout mouse models to selectively delete the transcription factor T-box 3 (Tbx3) in 1) astrocytes, 2) postnatal retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), or 3) retinal progenitors. We demonstrate that the hypovascular retina phenotype observed upon Tbx3 loss most likely stems from a disruption of early retinogenesis. Embryonic analyses revealed that TBX3 is required during a critical retinogenic window coinciding with ATOH7 activity. While ATOH7+ progenitors are more abundant in Tbx3 mutants, the expression of key RGC and cone precursor factors (including TBX5, RXRgamma, ISL1/2, POU4F2, SHH, LHX4 and OTX2) is severely diminished, halting proper RGC and cone differentiation. Utilizing birthdating experiments and developmental immunostaining, we establish TBX3 as a novel upstream regulator of RGC and cone photoreceptor specification. Because the degeneration of RGCs is the definitive hallmark of diseases like glaucoma, identifying TBX3 as a driver of early RGC formation positions it as a promising new candidate biomarker for early-stage glaucoma diagnosis and potentially therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: PRC2-binding regions are hotspots of DNA methylation entropy in pre-cancer and cancer
papers.abstract: DNA methylation aberrations and variability are pervasive features of cancer, yet their relationship with chromatin regulation remains incompletely understood. Across hundreds of matched tumor-normal methylomes, regions with the highest methylation entropy in both tumor and normal tissues were consistently enriched for PRC2-associated factors. In tumors, inter-sample methylation variability was increased across the full range of PRC2-associated levels, while mean methylation progressively increased from low- to high-PRC2-binding regions; this gradient was substantially weaker in matched normal tissues. PRC2-associated regions with higher DNA methylation levels were preferentially associated with poised and repressed chromatin states, reduced chromatin accessibility, and reduced gene expression. Independent normal-precancer-cancer cohorts showed that this PRC2-associated methylation state emerges early, with precancerous and malignant tissues displaying highly similar profiles that are distinct from those of healthy tissues. Single-cell colon cancer methylomes independently confirmed increased methylation entropy at PRC2 regions. Higher PRC2-region entropy was associated with scores reflecting hypoxic states, aggressive tumor features, and poorer survival outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify PRC2-binding regions as hotspots of DNA methylation variability that become dysregulated during tumorigenesis.

papers.title: An epigenetic palimpsest: the King penguin's blood methylome reveals conserved hematopoietic ageing
papers.abstract: Age-associated DNA methylation is conserved across vertebrates, but whether epigenetic ageing reflects cellular ageing programmes or age-dependent shifts in cell composition remains unresolved. Here, using 126 whole-blood methylomes from known-age King penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus), we exploit a vertebrate system in which nucleated erythrocytes dominate peripheral blood, minimizing the influence of leukocyte heterogeneity. We identify a core set of 409 ageing-associated genes showing lifelong, clock-like methylation change. These genes are strongly enriched for regulators of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) function and niche communication. Integration of methylome, transcriptome and chromatin-accessibility data reveals that many of the strongest ageing signals derive from genes inactive in mature erythrocytes, consistent with the persistence of epigenetic states from ancestral hematopoietic progenitors. A comparison with methylation profiles from 1,501 humans identified a conserved cross-species subset of ageing genes, and a human epigenetic age model constructed solely from orthologues of penguin ageing genes predicts chronological age with high accuracy while remaining largely insensitive to blood cell composition. We propose that blood epigenetic ageing signatures contain a long-lived cellular memory of stem-cell ageing, that may represent an evolutionarily ancient layer of the vertebrate ageing process.

papers.title: When can site-specific glycoform compositions resolve biosynthetic rates?
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry measures site-specific glycoform compositions, but when these measurements can resolve upstream biosynthetic rates remains unclear. We assess whether small changes in effective rates, each representing the processing capacity of a group of biosynthetic reactions, can be distinguished near specified baseline rates with secretion held fixed. Because proportions sum to one, m jointly normalised glycoform classes provide at most m-1 independent quantities. Distinguishing changes in k rates therefore requires at least k+1 classes, although this count alone does not ensure identifiability. In a canonical N-glycan network with eight rates, exhaustive evaluation of nine-class panels identified panels that could locally distinguish all eight rates. Among these panels, class choice changed the allowable measurement error by approximately 18-fold for the same target uncertainty in inferred rates. A separate simulation within the fixed network showed that estimating rate-change combinations with weaker composition responses reduced bias but amplified measurement noise. We applied the framework to plasma data from 40 controls and 70 patients across 14 inherited glycosylation-disorder groups. A prespecified composition score for the expected pathway disturbance ranked among the top two in 13 of 14 groups. Network responses linked observed composition shifts to biosynthetic reaction classes. Expanding site models from five to eight reaction classes improved control-composition fit but reduced the number of sites at which all modelled rates were locally distinguishable and increased noise sensitivity. Rate inference thus requires sufficient panel size, separable rate responses, adequate measurement precision and a model that fits the composition. These requirements guide measurement design and help determine whether compositions support pathway-level interpretation or individual-rate inference.

papers.title: Giant Vesicle Platform for Synthetic Endoplasmic Reticulum Networks
papers.abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a membrane-bound organelle found in all eukaryotic cells. This organelle has a fascinating morphology, which involves a network of membrane nanotubes and three-way junctions connecting three nanotubes. Previous reconstitution studies were based on proteo-liposomes with a size of 100 to 200 nanometers, using electron microscopy as the main method to image the resulting membrane morphologies. These studies revealed the importance of membrane GTPases, that is, membrane proteins that hydrolyse GTP. Here, we introduce an alternative platform for the formation of synthetic ER networks starting from giant unilamellar vesicles with a typical size of 10 mirometers and containing a single membrane GTPase such as atlastin from fruit flies or Sey1 from yeast. This giant vesicle approach makes the networks accessible to optical microscopy, by which one can elucidate both their structure and their dynamics. We first demonstrate that the membranes' propensity to form synthetic ER networks depends strongly on the lipid composition. More precisely, we show that this propensity varies non-monotonically with the mole fraction of cholesterol and that the frequency of three-way junctions has a maximum for an optimal mole fraction between 10 and 15 mol%. This optimal value is comparable to the mole fraction of cholesterol as estimated for ER membranes in vivo. We also demonstrate the formation of synthetic ER networks when the membranes contain only the membrane GTPase Sey1 but no other membrane protein, which implies that Sey1 is able on its own to generate a high membrane curvature. Based on the reconstitution approach introduced here, the synthetic ER networks can now be further investigated using the versatile toolbox that has been developed for giant vesicles.

papers.title: Catalase import into peroxisomes in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: In eukaryotes, catalases are peroxisomal antioxidant enzymes that maintain cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis. Plant catalases lack canonical peroxisomal targeting signals (PTS), and the mechanism underlying their PEX5-dependent peroxisomal import remains poorly understood. Here, we expressed CAT2 with N- and C-terminal GFP fusions in an Arabidopsis cat2 mutant background and found that only GFP-CAT2 completely restored wild-type function despite comparable catalase activity for both CAT2-GFP and GFP-CAT2. Only GFP-CAT2 localized to peroxisomes, indicating that altered subcellular localization prevented CAT2-GFP functional complementation. Expression of CAT2-GFP in wild-type Arabidopsis and Nicotiana benthamiana revealed in vivo interaction with endogenous catalases leading to co-import into peroxisomes. Localization of YFP fused to various CAT2 C-terminal sections identified the CAT2 C-terminal five amino acids as a functional PTS1-like sequence. These findings define a minimal C-terminal targeting motif for plant catalases that is sufficient for their peroxisomal import.

papers.title: Genome-wide association study in a maize diversity panel dissects the genetic basis of lignocellulosic recalcitrance
papers.abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is an abundant, renewable resource for the production of biorenewable products. Its efficient utilization is largely hindered by the inherent recalcitrance of lignocellulose to degradation. Natural genetic variation in biomass saccharification efficiency and lignocellulose components across diverse maize germplasm provides a powerful resource to dissect the genetic basis of lignocellulosic recalcitrance. Here, we performed high-throughput profiling of lignocellulosic components and saccharification efficiency in mature stalks across a diverse panel of 239 field grown maize inbred lines, and identified extensive natural variation in biomass properties. Saccharification efficiency was strongly positively associated with matrix glucose content, moderately positively associated with the arabinose-to-xylose (Ara:Xyl) molar ratio and crystalline cellulose content, whereas saccharification efficiency was strongly negatively associated with xylose and lignin content. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) were conducted to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with saccharification efficiency and lignocellulosic components. Numerous significant single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified, defining 79 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) across all 10 maize chromosomes. The presence of pleiotropic SNPs and the extensive co-localization of QTLs for multiple traits highlight the complex genetic architecture and shared genetic basis of maize biomass properties. Our study reveals substantial natural variation in maize biomass digestibility and identifies multiple novel genetic loci underlying variation in saccharification efficiency and lignocellulose components.

papers.title: Ancestral State Reconstruction under Localized Evolutionary Change: Error Patterns and Their Control by Tree Partitioning
papers.abstract: Localized evolutionary changes can distort ancestral state reconstruction (ASR) because conventional continuous-trait methods generally treat branchwise changes as draws from a shared background process. A disproportionately large change confined to a single branch therefore creates localized model misspecification, but how the resulting errors vary among reconstruction paradigms and phylogenetic positions remains poorly understood. Using controlled simulations on idealized and empirical mammalian phylogenies, we characterized the error patterns produced by single-branch large changes (SBLCs) across five Brownian-motion-based ASR implementations. On intact trees, errors were highly structured and method dependent: the recursive local method propagated distortion mainly upstream, whereas global methods produced multidirectional effects involving both SBLC boundary nodes, neighboring lineages, and descendants of the affected branch. We then evaluated patching, a conditional robustness procedure that partitions the phylogeny at a candidate branch, applies the same ASR method independently to the resulting subtrees, and estimates the upstream boundary node state by branch-length-weighted interpolation. Patching reduced errors near and away from the affected branch and lowered tree-wide error across trait-increasing and trait-decreasing SBLCs, a broad range of sensitivity analyses, and configurations with two co-occurring SBLCs, while introducing little additional error when no SBLC was present. Under the reference upsizing SBLC, for instance, it cut the maximum-likelihood reconstruction error at the upstream boundary node from 56.20 to 0.03 (mean true state, 4.98), matching the stable-process benchmark. In cetacean body-length evolution, patching candidate branches identified by a Levy-process model generally shifted conventional estimates toward stable-process estimates and nearby fossil references. Under an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with strong post-SBLC mean reversion, however, neither patching nor stable-process reconstruction recovered downstream ancestral states once the phenotypic signature of the SBLC had largely disappeared from descendant tip values, revealing an identifiability limit of terminal-only inference. Localized evolutionary change therefore creates structured, method-dependent reconstruction errors, and tree partitioning provides a complementary diagnostic of the robustness of ancestral inferences to candidate branch-localized changes.

papers.title: Direct 3D isolation in gelatin methacryloyl microbeads versus conventional 2D isolation and culture: a trade-off between mesenchymal stromal cell purity and niche-associated transcriptional profiles
papers.abstract: Bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) isolation typically couples plastic-adherence selection to planar expansion. Therefore, the recovered cells may reflect culture adaptation as much as native stromal biology. Direct isolation within a three-dimensional matrix could reduce planar selection, but its effects on cellular recovery, composition and MSC transcriptional profiles remain insufficiently resolved. We therefore developed a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) workflow progressing from bulk hydrogels to medium-surrounded GelMA microbeads (GMBs) and compared 3D-derived cells with conventional 2D cultures. Qualitative live/dead staining with calcein acetoxymethyl ester (CAM) and propidium iodide (PI) and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) imaging established cellular activity in both GelMA formats. In bulk GelMA cultures from four human donors, CD73-, CD90- and CD105-associated flow-cytometric readouts did not increase from day 7 to day 21. At day 21, the combined marker readout was numerically higher in donor-matched 2D cultures than in bulk 3D cultures, which retained heterogeneous marker-defined populations. GMBs enabled cell recovery and flow-cytometric characterization and motivated an exploratory one-donor single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. The final dataset contained 37,784 cells across four samples and 23 annotated populations. MSC-focused re-embedding resolved 13,175 cells into two 3D and four 2D clusters. A pooled comparison identified 4,840 differentially expressed genes (DEGs, false discovery rate [FDR]<0.01, |log2FC|[≥]1), indicating a broad method-associated expression shift. The 3D C1 cluster combined progenitor-, extracellular-matrix-, adhesion-, cytokine-, hypoxia/glycolysis- and predicted-interaction-associated programmes, whereas 2D clusters showed mitochondrial, cytoskeletal/mechanoadaptive and proliferative programmes. Thus, 2D culture yielded a more strongly represented and compositionally purer MSC compartment, while 3D isolation contained rare MSC clusters with niche-associated transcriptional profiles within a heterogeneous marrow environment. These findings support a testable native-associated tendency for 3D, but donor replication, matched recovery and direct native-reference mapping are required before inferring greater in-vivo similarity or functional superiority.

papers.title: A single epigenetic repressor controls opposing developmental tempos in human neural and cranial neural crest lineages
papers.abstract: The precise timing of lineage specification is essential for embryonic development, yet the epigenetic mechanisms enforcing human developmental tempo remain poorly understood. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ZNF462 cause Weiss-Kruszka syndrome (WKS), a pleiotropic disorder characterized by neurodevelopmental delays and craniofacial dysmorphisms. Here, we show that ZNF462 acts as an epigenetic gatekeeper that coordinates human developmental tempo across divergent lineages by repressing cell lineage-specific gene enhancers. In human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), ZNF462 maintains self-renewal by recruiting the G9A/GLP histone methyltransferase complex to silence primate-specific retrotransposon-derived enhancers. Upon neural lineage commitment, ZNF462 redirects to hominoid-specific LTR5_Hs elements and divergent lineage-specific enhancer programs, where its loss produces opposing kinetics. In neural progenitor cells (NPCs), ZNF462 enforces G9A/GLP-dependent repression of ZIC-driven neural enhancers, and loss of this repression traps NPCs in a progenitor state, slowing cortical neurogenesis without impairing terminal neurogenic capacity. In neural crest cells (NCCs), ZNF462 targets repressive chromatin to silence SOX9 family-driven enhancers. Here, ZNF462 haploinsufficiency triggers premature activation of definitive NCC specifiers, accelerating differentiation. These findings establish that a single repressor can simultaneously decelerate and accelerate developmental tempo by gating lineage-specific enhancers, placing Weiss-Kruszka syndrome into the emerging class of human developmental timing disorders.

papers.title: Reversible fixation of microbial cells for targeted genomics
papers.abstract: Phylogeny- or activity-based fluorescent labelling of microorganisms coupled with fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) is a powerful approach to rapidly isolate cells of interest from complex communities for targeted genomics. However, the method has not been widely adopted because standard paraformaldehyde or ethanol fixation procedures hamper nucleic acid recovery and/or long-term sample storage. Here, we present dithiobis(succinimidyl propionate) (DSP) as a reversible fixative for microbial cells that enables fluorescence imaging and DNA extraction and amplification for sequencing. DSP fixation is compatible with widely used fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) approaches and bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging, and can be applied to diverse sample types, where it consistently performed as well as paraformaldehyde. Furthermore, high-quality genomes were obtained from individual and multiple bacterial cells selectively extracted from complex samples using FISH-FACS. Thus, DSP is a dual-use fixative for microbiome imaging and sequencing, improving targeted microbial genomics.

papers.title: Viral dispersal drives changes in population composition
papers.abstract: In an acute viral infection, a small seeding population expands rapidly over several orders of magnitude, then declines. This vast population growth is accompanied by spatial expansion as infection spreads to new anatomical sites within the host. Evolutionary theory predicts that spatially expanding populations experience more extreme stochastic losses of genetic diversity than spatially unstructured populations. To test this prediction in the context of viral dynamics, we evaluated the impact of spatial expansion on viral population genetic structure and assessed how modulators of viral dispersal affected this structure. To this end, we developed a means of implementing the spatial expansion of influenza A virus in cell culture and applied it to a viral population carrying a diverse genetic barcode. Across this simplified cellular landscape, we found that spatial expansion produces a patchwork of distinct viral subpopulations. We then evaluated the consequences for population structure of two modulators of viral dispersal: extracellular viscosity and a common polymorphism in the viral attachment protein. Both physical constraint and viral phenotype altered the extent of genetic bottlenecking and spatial heterogeneity that developed during expansion, indicating that environmental features and viral traits that modulate dispersal also modulate viral population composition, diversity and evolution.
